nodes.name: Hilbert's Tenth Problem over Q and for bounded complexity
nodes.statement: However, the problem remains open when generalized to the field of rational numbers, or contrarily, when restricted to Diophantine equations with bounded complexity, characterized by the number of variables $\nu$ and the degree $\delta$.

nodes.name: Hilbert's Tenth Problem
nodes.statement: The tenth problem on David Hilbert's 1900 list of twenty-three mathematical problems asks for an algorithm to decide the solvability of any arbitrary Diophantine equation~\cite{hilbert-problems}.
nodes.statement_short: Find an algorithm deciding solvability of an arbitrary Diophantine equation.

nodes.name: Diophantine equation
nodes.statement: A \emph{Diophantine equation} is a multivariate polynomial equation over the integers.

nodes.name: Parameter and unknowns of a parametric equation
nodes.statement: One often considers parametric equations of the type $P(a, z_1, \ldots, z_\nu)=0$ where $a$ is called the parameter and $z_1, \ldots, z_\nu$ are called unknowns.

nodes.name: Diophantine set
nodes.statement: A \emph{Diophantine set} $A \subset {\mathbb N}$ is then defined to be any set of parameters such that $a \in A$ if and only if there are unknowns $z_1, \ldots, z_\nu \in {\mathbb Z}$ with $P(a, z_1, \ldots, z_\nu) = 0$.
differentia: $a \in A$ if and only if there are unknowns $z_1, \ldots, z_\nu \in {\mathbb Z}$ with $P(a, z_1, \ldots, z_\nu) = 0$

nodes.name: Davis-Putnam-Robinson-Matiyasevich theorem
nodes.statement: The Davis-Putnam-Robinson-Matiyasevich theorem (1970)~\cite[Chapter~1]{matiyasevich-book} states that every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine; this is a deep relation between number theory and computability theory.
conclusions: every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine

nodes.name: Diophantine sets are recursively enumerable
nodes.statement: An enumeration argument shows that, conversely, every Diophantine set is recursively enumerable.
conclusions: every Diophantine set is recursively enumerable

nodes.name: Undecidability of Hilbert's Tenth Problem
nodes.statement: The resulting equivalence implies that there are Diophantine sets which are not decidable, and hence proves that Hilbert's Tenth Problem is undecidable.
also_stated_at: Hilbert's Tenth Problem was answered negatively by Yuri Matiyasevich, who showed that there is no general algorithm to decide whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation has a solution.
conclusions: there are Diophantine sets which are not decidable
Hilbert's Tenth Problem is undecidable

nodes.name: universal Diophantine equation
nodes.statement: Because the set of all recursively enumerable (r.e.) sets is itself recursively enumerable, there must exist a corresponding Diophantine equation for this set, representing all r.e. sets, i.e. all Diophantine sets at once. An equation with this property is known as a \emph{universal Diophantine equation}, and an explicit example can be found in an article by Jones~\cite{9var}.
differentia: representing all r.e. sets, i.e. all Diophantine sets at once

nodes.name: universal pair
nodes.statement: If all Diophantine sets can be represented by a polynomial in at most $\nu$ unknowns and in degree at most $\delta$, we call $(\nu, \delta)$ a \emph{universal pair}.
also_stated_at: If every Diophantine set can be represented within the bounds $(\nu, \delta)$, we say that this pair is \emph{universal}, and it follows that the corresponding class of equations is undecidable.

nodes.name: Universal pairs over N and over Z
nodes.statement: Universal pairs can be defined for both cases, and we shall write $(\nu, \delta)_{\mathbb N}$ and $(\nu, \delta)_{\mathbb Z}$ to make the distinction explicit.

nodes.name: Jones' universal pair (9, 1.64e45)
nodes.statement: Jones~\cite{9var} later published a complete proof that $(9, 1.64 \cdot 10^{45})_{\mathbb N}$ is universal, together with the lowest currently known degree $\delta = 4$.
conclusions: $(9, 1.64 \cdot 10^{45})_{\mathbb N}$ is universal

nodes.name: Jones' universal pair (58, 4)
nodes.statement: More precisely, the pair $(58, 4)_{\mathbb N}$ is universal, too.
conclusions: the pair $(58, 4)_{\mathbb N}$ is universal

nodes.name: Universal pairs over N induce pairs over Z
nodes.statement: Note that any universal pair over ${\mathbb N}$ induces a pair over ${\mathbb Z}$.
conclusions: any universal pair over ${\mathbb N}$ induces a pair over ${\mathbb Z}$

nodes.name: Lagrange's four square theorem
nodes.statement: Every $n \in {\mathbb N}$ can be written as $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2$ for integers $x,y,z,w \in {\mathbb Z}$ using Lagrange's four square theorem.
conclusions: can be written as $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2$ for integers $x,y,z,w \in {\mathbb Z}$

nodes.name: Four-squares conversion from N to Z unknowns
nodes.statement: Thus, a Diophantine equation with unknowns in ${\mathbb N}$ can be transformed into an equation with unknowns in ${\mathbb Z}$ by introducing additional unknowns. However, this conversion gives bounds that are far from optimal.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute a sum of four integer squares for each natural-number unknown.

nodes.name: Unknown counts from four- and three-squares substitutions
nodes.statement: Using the four-squares substitution for $\nu = 9$ over the natural numbers would thus require 36 integer unknowns. A more efficient substitution is possible using the more sophisticated three squares theorem (cf. \cref{sec:three-squares}); this would yield universality for 27 integer unknowns.
nodes.statement_short: Four-squares substitution from 9 natural unknowns gives 36 integer unknowns; three squares gives 27.

nodes.name: Universal pair (11, eta(nu, delta)) over Z
nodes.section: 1.3 First Nontrivial Bounds over \texorpdfstring{${\mathbb Z}$}{the Integers}
conclusions: In particular, \[ (11,1.16258\cdot 10^{63})_{\mathbb Z} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (11, 9.19593 \cdot 10^{53})_{\mathbb Z} \] are universal over ${\mathbb Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Any universal pair $(\nu,\delta)_{\mathbb N}$ yields a universal pair over $\mathbb Z$ with 11 unknowns and explicit degree $\eta(\nu,\delta)$.
nodes.label: thm:11-universal-pair

nodes.name: Comparison of the two universal pairs
nodes.statement: Observe that, in principle, the second pair stated above is better than the first. We state both because the second pair depends on Jones' universal pair $(32, 12)_{\mathbb N}$ of which there is no published proof in the literature. The first pair depends instead on $(58, 4)_{\mathbb N}$.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Nontrivial Bounds over \texorpdfstring{${\mathbb Z}$}{the Integers}
nodes.statement_short: The better pair relies on Jones' unpublished $(32,12)_{\mathbb N}$; the other on $(58,4)_{\mathbb N}$.

nodes.name: Corollary 1 from Theorem 1
nodes.statement: \cref{thm:11-universal-pair} implies the following stronger response to Hilbert's Tenth Problem.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Nontrivial Bounds over \texorpdfstring{${\mathbb Z}$}{the Integers}
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of Theorem 1 (universality implies undecidability).

nodes.name: Hilbert's Tenth Problem unsolvable for 11 unknowns
nodes.statement: Consider the class of Diophantine equations with at most 11 unknowns and at most degree $1.63 \cdot 10^{63}$. Hilbert's Tenth Problem is unsolvable for this class: There is no algorithm that can determine for all equations in this class whether they have a solution or not.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Nontrivial Bounds over \texorpdfstring{${\mathbb Z}$}{the Integers}
assumptions: Consider the class of Diophantine equations with at most 11 unknowns and at most degree $1.63 \cdot 10^{63}$.
conclusions: Hilbert's Tenth Problem is unsolvable for this class: There is no algorithm that can determine for all equations in this class whether they have a solution or not.
nodes.label: cor:strong-htp

nodes.name: Sun's eleven unknowns theorem
nodes.statement: In particular, he proved that any Diophantine equation can be reduced to an equivalent one with only eleven integer unknowns.
conclusions: any Diophantine equation can be reduced to an equivalent one with only eleven integer unknowns

nodes.name: multivariate polynomial type mpoly
nodes.statement: The type of multivariate polynomials is defined as \begin{align} \alpha\; \texttt{mpoly} := ({\mathbb N} \Rightarrow_0 {\mathbb N}) \Rightarrow_0 \alpha \end{align} for any type $\alpha$ with a zero.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomials as finitely supported maps from monomials (finite exponent assignments) to coefficients.

nodes.name: mpoly type definition
nodes.statement: \alpha\; \texttt{mpoly} := ({\mathbb N} \Rightarrow_0 {\mathbb N}) \Rightarrow_0 \alpha
nodes.label: eq:typedef-mpoly

nodes.name: finite assignment
nodes.statement: We use $\beta \Rightarrow_0 \alpha$ to denote a \emph{finite assignment}, i.e. a function from $\beta$ to $\alpha$ that takes only finitely many nonzero values.
differentia: takes only finitely many nonzero values

nodes.name: mpoly inherits ring structure
nodes.statement: Of course, this type inherits much algebraic structure from the underlying coefficient type: if $\alpha$ is a ring or an integral domain, then so is $\alpha$ \texttt{mpoly}.
assumptions: $\alpha$ is a ring or an integral domain
conclusions: so is $\alpha$ \texttt{mpoly}

nodes.statement:
P(z_0, \ldots, z_
u) = \sum_{i_0, \ldots, i_
u \, \in \, {\mathbb N}} c_{i_0, \ldots, i_
u} \prod_{s=0}^

nodes.label: eq:multivariate-expansion

nodes.name: multi-index and its norm
nodes.statement:
Below, we abbreviate the indices with a single multi-index $\mathbf{i} = (i_0, \ldots, i_
u) \in {\mathbb N}^{
u+1}$, defining $\|\mathbf{i}\| := \sum_{s=0}^

nodes.statement:
P(z_0, \ldots, z_

nodes.label: eq:multivariate-expansion-bounded

nodes.name: Notational conventions for Isabelle pseudo-code
nodes.statement: In the interest of legibility, throughout the paper, we are presenting Isabelle-style pseudo-code in which we have dropped some notation that is syntactically but not semantically necessary. Moreover, by writing \texttt{||i||} above we mean the library function \texttt{sum\_list i}. We write $\alpha$ for the free type variable \texttt{'a} representing the ring of coefficients. We assume $\alpha$~\texttt{::} \texttt{comm\_ring\_1}, a commutative and unital ring, throughout.
nodes.statement_short: Isabelle pseudo-code drops syntactic noise; ||i|| is sum_list; alpha is a commutative unital ring.

nodes.name: Injections lift to mpoly
nodes.statement: For example, we formalize that if one type injects into a larger type like ${\mathbb Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$, then the same holds for ${\mathbb Z}$ \texttt{mpoly} $\hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ \texttt{mpoly}.
assumptions: one type injects into a larger type like ${\mathbb Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$
conclusions: the same holds for ${\mathbb Z}$ \texttt{mpoly} $\hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ \texttt{mpoly}

nodes.name: poly_subst_monom
nodes.statement: definition poly_subst_monom :: "(nat$\Rightarrow$$\alpha$ mpoly) $\Rightarrow$ (nat$\Rightarrow_0$nat) $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ mpoly" where "poly_subst_monom f m = $\prod$s. (f s) ^ (m s)"

nodes.name: poly_subst (polynomial substitution)
nodes.statement: definition poly_subst :: "(nat$\Rightarrow$$\alpha$ mpoly) $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ mpoly $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ mpoly" where "poly_subst f P = $\sum$m. (Const (coeff P m)) * poly_subst_monom f m"
nodes.statement_short: Substitute polynomials f_s for each variable via the coefficient expansion of P.

nodes.name: Substitution as a list of polynomials
nodes.statement:
In standard mathematical notation, given a polynomial $P \in {\mathbb Z}[z_0, \ldots, z_
u]$, we would write this substitution as a list of $(
u+1)$-many polynomials $f = (f_0, \ldots, f_
u) \in {\mathbb Z}[z_0, \ldots, z_
u]^{
u+1}$.

nodes.name: Substitution commutes with evaluation
also_stated_at: lemma insertion_poly_subst: "insertion z (poly_subst f P) = insertion ((insertion z) $\circ$ f) P"
assumptions: given a vector of integers $\mathbf{z} = (z_0, \ldots, z_\nu) \in {\mathbb Z}^{\nu+1}$
conclusions: P(f)(\mathbf{z}) = P(f(\mathbf{z})),
nodes.statement_short: Evaluating a substituted polynomial equals evaluating P at the evaluated substitutions.

nodes.name: Substitution-evaluation identity
nodes.statement: P(f)(\mathbf{z}) = P(f(\mathbf{z})),
nodes.label: eq:substitution-evaluation

nodes.name: insertion (evaluation morphism)
nodes.statement: In Isabelle, the evaluation morphism is formalized as \texttt{insertion z P} for an assignment of the type \texttt{z :\!\!\! nat $\Rightarrow \alpha$} and a multivariate polynomial \texttt{P :\! $\alpha$ mpoly}.

nodes.name: vars
nodes.statement: lift_definition vars :: "$\alpha$ mpoly $\Rightarrow$ nat set" is "$\lambda$P. $\bigcup$ (keys ` keys P)"

nodes.name: max_vars
nodes.statement: definition max_vars :: "$\alpha$ mpoly $\Rightarrow$ nat" where "max_vars P $\equiv$ Max (insert 0 (vars P))"

nodes.name: total_degree
nodes.statement: lift_definition total_degree :: "$\alpha$ mpoly $\Rightarrow$ nat" is "$\lambda$P. Max (insert 0 (($\lambda$m. sum (lookup m) (keys m)) ` keys P))"

nodes.name: keys
nodes.statement: The morphism \texttt{keys} is defined to be the set of all elements of the domain which are mapped to a non-zero value. In particular, \texttt{keys P} is the set of all monomials which appear in $P$ with non-zero coefficient.

nodes.name: Degree of the zero polynomial
nodes.statement: The definition of \texttt{total\_degree} works in analogy to \texttt{max\_vars}. Because the zero polynomial has \texttt{keys (Const 0)} $= \emptyset$, we again include \texttt{insert 0}. However, this formalizes the degree of the zero polynomial as~$0$. A consequence of this definition is, e.g., that the assumptions $P \neq 0$ and $Q \neq 0$ are now required for the lemma \texttt{total\_degree (P * Q) = total\_degree P + total\_degree Q}.
nodes.statement_short: The zero polynomial gets degree 0, so multiplicativity of degree needs nonzero factors.

nodes.name: Subadditivity of total degree under multiplication
nodes.statement: Indeed, \texttt{total\_degree (P * Q) $\leq$ total\_degree P + total\_degree Q} is true without any assumptions on $P$ or $Q$.
conclusions: \texttt{total\_degree (P * Q) $\leq$ total\_degree P + total\_degree Q}

nodes.name: degree P s
nodes.statement: Note that \texttt{degree P s} calculates the degree of $P$ in the variable $z_s$ only.

nodes.name: Relative bounds for poly_subst (vars_poly_subst, total_degree_poly_subst)
nodes.statement: lemma vars_poly_subst: "vars (poly_subst f P) $\subseteq$ $\bigcup$s $\in$ vars P. vars (f s)" (* Proof omitted *) \end{lstlisting} \needspace{4\baselineskip} \begin{lstlisting} lemma total_degree_poly_subst: "total_degree (poly_subst f P) $\leq$ $\sum$s $\in$ vars P. degree P s * total_degree (f s)"
conclusions: vars (poly_subst f P) $\subseteq$ $\bigcup$s $\in$ vars P. vars (f s)
$\leq$ $\sum$s $\in$ vars P. degree P s * total_degree (f s)
nodes.statement_short: Variables of a substitution lie in the union of the substituted polynomials' variables; its degree is bounded by sum of degree-in-$z_s$ times degree of $f_s$.

nodes.name: poly_extract
nodes.statement: Using this framework, a polynomial $P$ is initially formalized as a standard Isabelle term of type \lstinline{P :: int => int => ... => int}. The command \texttt{poly\_extract P} then generates a new term \texttt{P\_poly} of type \texttt{int mpoly} and automatically proves a lemma \texttt{P\_correct}. This lemma guarantees that evaluating \texttt{P\_poly} yields the same result as evaluating the original function \texttt{P}. The extraction succeeds if \texttt{P} is a valid polynomial: constructed from integer constants and variables, addition, multiplication, and any polynomial term \texttt{C} for which a corresponding correctness lemma \texttt{C\_correct} exists.

output: a new term \texttt{P\_poly} of type \texttt{int mpoly}

nodes.name: Three squares theorem
nodes.statement: The three squares theorem states that for every $n \in {\mathbb N}$ there exist integers $x, y, z \in {\mathbb Z}$ such that $n = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + z$.
conclusions: there exist integers $x, y, z \in {\mathbb Z}$ such that $n = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + z$

nodes.name: Combining x > 0 and y != 0
nodes.statement: The idea of relation-combining is the following: imagine we want to check the two conditions $x > 0, y \ne 0$ with Diophantine polynomials in integer variables. A naive method would use the three-squares formula for each condition, i.e. the conditions are true if \begin{align*} x &= a^2+b^2+c^2+c+1 \\ y^2 &= d^2+e^2+f^2+f+1 \end{align*} for some $a,b,c,d,e,f \in {\mathbb Z}$. However, there is a more efficient method because the two conditions together are equivalent to the single condition \[ xy^2 = a^2+b^2+c^2+c+1 \;, \] using only $a, b, c \in {\mathbb Z}$, cutting the number of integer variables required in half.
nodes.statement_short: Two positivity/nonzero conditions combined into one three-squares condition $xy^2 = a^2+b^2+c^2+c+1$.

nodes.name: Matiyasevich-Robinson relation-combining lemma
nodes.statement: For every $q>0$ there is a polynomial $M_q$ with the property that for all integers $A_1,\dots,A_q,R,S,T$ such that $S\neq 0$, the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $S|T$, $R>0$ and $A_1,\dots,A_q$ are squares, \item $\exists n \ge 0 : \, M_q(A_1,\dots,A_q,S,T,R,n)=0$. \end{enumerate} Specifically, $M_q$ can be given as \begin{equation} \begin{split} &M_q(A_1,\dots,A_q,S,T,R,n)\\ &=\prod_{\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_q\in\{\pm1\}^q}\left(S^2n + T^2 - S^2(2R-1)\left(T^2 + X_q^q +\sum_{j=1}^q \varepsilon_j \sqrt{A_j}X_q^{j-1}\right) \right) \\ \end{split} \end{equation} where $X_q:=1+\sum_{j=1}^{q}A_j^2$.
also_stated_at: lemma relation_combining: assumes "S $\neq$ 0" shows "(S dvd T $\wedge$ R > 0 $\wedge$ is_square A${}_1$ $\wedge$ is_square A${}_2$ $\wedge$ is_square A${}_3$) = ($\exists$n$\geq$0. M3 A${}_1$ A${}_2$ A${}_3$ S T R n = 0)"
conclusions: there is a polynomial $M_q$ with the property that for all integers $A_1,\dots,A_q,R,S,T$ such that $S\neq 0$, the following are equivalent:
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility, positivity and q squareness conditions combine into one polynomial $M_q$ with one natural unknown.
nodes.label: lem:relation-combining

nodes.name: Matiyasevich polynomial M_q
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &M_q(A_1,\dots,A_q,S,T,R,n)\\ &=\prod_{\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_q\in\{\pm1\}^q}\left(S^2n + T^2 - S^2(2R-1)\left(T^2 + X_q^q +\sum_{j=1}^q \varepsilon_j \sqrt{A_j}X_q^{j-1}\right) \right) \\ \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:matiyasevich-polynomial

nodes.name: M_q is a polynomial
nodes.statement: The short-hand notation in equation~\eqref{eq:matiyasevich-polynomial} defines a polynomial because $M_q$ is even in $\sqrt{A_j}$.

nodes.name: Diophantine operation
nodes.statement: Crucially, all operations appearing in the intermediate expressions must be Diophantine, that is, expressible using polynomials.

nodes.name: Divisibility, congruence and inequalities are Diophantine
nodes.statement: Many fundamental mathematical relations admit such representations~\cite{matiyasevich-book}, including divisibility, congruence modulo an integer, and inequalities.
conclusions: Many fundamental mathematical relations admit such representations~\cite{matiyasevich-book}, including divisibility, congruence modulo an integer, and inequalities.

nodes.name: Exponentiation, binomial coefficients and factorials are Diophantine
nodes.statement: Relations involving exponentiation, binomial coefficients and factorials also admit Diophantine representations.
conclusions: Relations involving exponentiation, binomial coefficients and factorials also admit Diophantine representations.

nodes.statement: It is possible to define a number $\alpha_P$ such that the product $K = (1 + c)^{\deg P} \cdot \alpha_P$ contains the value $P(z_1, \ldots, z_\nu)$ in a specific location of its base $\mathscr{B}$ expansion.

nodes.name: From digits to binomial divisibility
nodes.statement: One can therefore translate the statement $P(z_1, \ldots, z_\nu) = 0$ into a statement about the base $\mathscr{B}$ expansion of $K$. Ensuring that a certain base $\mathscr{B}$ digit of $K$ is zero can then be encoded by counting carries during binary addition. In turn, this condition can be translated into a divisibility condition on a binomial coefficient~\cite[Lemmas~1.3 and~1.4]{manuscript}.
nodes.statement_short: P(z)=0 becomes a zero digit of K, encoded via carry counting and then a binomial-coefficient divisibility.

All quantities depend on a given polynomial $P \in {\mathbb Z}[a, z_1, \ldots, z_\nu]$ with parameter $a$ and $\nu$ unknowns.

nodes.name: Lucas sequence
nodes.statement: A \emph{Lucas sequence with parameter $A\in{\mathbb Z}$} is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in {\mathbb Z}}$ that satisfies the recursive relation \begin{equation} x_{n+1}=Ax_n-x_{n-1}. \end{equation} Each such sequence is defined uniquely by two initial values, and we define two particular Lucas sequences with initial values $\psi_0(A)=0, \psi_1(A)=1$ as well as $\chi_0(A)=2, \chi_1(A)=A$.

nodes.name: Lucas sequences at negative indices
nodes.statement: We then extend this recursive definition to all $n \in {\mathbb Z}$ by using the symmetries of these sequences, given by $\psi_{-n}(A) = -\psi_n(A)$ and $\chi_{-n}(A) = \chi_n(A)$.

nodes.name: Exponential growth of Lucas sequences
nodes.statement: These two second-order recurrences grow exponentially: for example, if $n \ge 2$ and $A>1$, we have $(A-1)^n < \psi_{n+1}(A) < A^n$.

nodes.name: Bridge variables and relations
nodes.statement: Given variables $X,Y,b,g,h,k,l,w,x,y$ we define the following variables: \begin{subequations} \begin{align} U &:= 2lXY \\ V &:= 4gwY \\ A &:= U(V+1) \\ B &:= 2X+1 \\ C &:= B+(A-2)h \\ D &:= (A^2-4)C^2+4 \\ E &:= C^2Dx \\ F &:= 4(A^2-4)E^2+1 \\ G &:= 1+CDF-2(A+2)(A-2)^2E^2 \\ H &:= C+BF+(2y-1)CF \\ I &:= (G^2-1)H^2+1 \\ J &:= X+1+k(U^2V-2) \end{align} \end{subequations} Denote the set of squares by $\square$. We define the following relations on the just-constructed variables: \begin{subequations} \begin{align} &DFI \in \square \\ &(U^{4}V^2-4)J^2+4\in\square \\ &(2A-5) \,\big|\, (3bwC-2(b^2w^2-1)) \\ & \left(\frac{C}{J}-lY\right)^2 < \frac{1}{16g^2} \;. \end{align} \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (eleven unknowns)
nodes.statement: By the Three Squares Theorem, any $n \geq 0$ can be represented as $n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2 + n_3$. Therefore, $\tilde Q$ has a solution whenever $n \geq 0$ and $Q$ has a solution, i.e. when \eqref{eq:Q-solution} holds. Using \cref{thm:9-unknowns-ZN}, we can thus deduce that $P$ has a solution whenever $\tilde Q$ has a solution. The preceding construction uses exactly 11 unknowns, completing the proof of~\cref{thm:11-unknowns}.
